topIssues.title: Remove Karst-specific upgrade transactions from GenerateNUTBundle
topIssues.author: 0xniha
topIssues.body:
**Description**
After the Karst upgrade is deployed to all networks, the Karst-specific upgrade transactions in `GenerateNUTBundle.s.sol` should be removed as they're only needed for that upgrade.

**Transactions to Remove**

In `_preImplementationDeployments()` (lines 169-172):
- ConditionalDeployer implementation deployment
- ConditionalDeployer proxy upgrade

In `_preL2CMDeployment()` (lines 184-187):
- L2ProxyAdmin upgrade transaction

The Karst conditional checks and associated helper functions (`_generateConditionalDeployerTxns`, `_generateL2ProxyAdminUpgrade`) can be removed once all chains have completed the Karst upgrade.

topIssues.title: [L2CM] Disable upgrades to V5 initializers
topIssues.author: maurelian
topIssues.body:
OPContractsManagerUtils.upgrade tries to reject OpenZeppelin v5 Initializable contracts by checking the caller-supplied slot and the target proxy's ERC-7201 initializer slot before the final upgrade. That only detects proxies that already have v5 initializer state.

A proxy that currently uses the v4 layout has an empty ERC-7201 slot, so it passes the guard. If the incoming implementation uses the v5 initializer layout, upgradeAndCall then delegates to its initializer and writes _initialized into the ERC-7201 slot. The helper has now installed an implementation that its own guard says is unsupported.

Consequently, the next standard OPCM upgrade for that proxy reverts before it can repair or replace the implementation, because the same guard now sees the nonzero ERC-7201 slot. A single release that accidentally includes a v5-style implementation can leave the proxy outside the normal OPCM upgrade mechanism until a custom recovery helper or manual storage fix is used.

Example:

A proxy currently points to a v4-style implementation.
The proxy's v5 ERC-7201 initializer slot is empty.
A release accidentally provides a v5-style implementation.
OPContractsManagerUtils.upgrade checks the v5 slot and sees bytes32(0), so it does not revert.
The helper clears the old v4 initializer byte.
The helper calls upgradeAndCall with the new implementation.
The new implementation's initializer writes to the v5 ERC-7201 initializer slot.
The upgrade succeeds, even though OPCM says v5 initializer state is unsupported.
The next standard OPCM upgrade checks the same v5 slot, now sees a nonzero value, and reverts with OPContractsManagerUtils_OZv5InitializableUnsupported.
Recommendation
Make the unsupported initializer-layout rule apply to the incoming implementation before it is installed. If OPCM intends to reject v5 initializers, require release implementations to expose a supported-layout marker or enforce an implementation codehash/metadata allowlist that upgrade can check before upgradeAndCall.

If v5 implementations should be allowed, support that layout deliberately instead: clear the ERC-7201 _initialized field and check the v5 _initializing flag.

topIssues.title: op-supernode: gate per-chain RPC during virtual node pause-and-restart
topIssues.author: wwared
topIssues.body:
## Summary

When op-supernode tears down a chain's virtual node (VN) during an interop reorg that invalidates a block and triggers an EL rewind, the per-chain JSON-RPC endpoint returns transient errors for the duration of the teardown-and-restart even though, from an operator's perspective, the chain is recovering normally. Any RPC consumer (op-conductor, monitoring, ops scripts) observes this as a hard outage and may react accordingly. Holding requests across the transition window, instead of failing them, would model the situation more accurately and avoid spurious "RPC down" signals downstream.

Interop reorgs are expected to be exceedingly uncommon in normal operation — they indicate something has already gone wrong upstream. The motivation for this issue is that when one does occur, the supernode's own recovery flow shouldn't simultaneously look like a separate outage to every consumer of the RPC.

## Problem

The chain container deliberately stops and rebuilds the VN around an interop reorg to prevent peer-chain VNs from racing ahead of a pending rewind. The interop activity calls `PauseAndStopVN` on **all** chains before invalidating any block (`op-supernode/supernode/activity/interop/interop.go:704-716`), then resumes them once invalidation completes.

During that window, the supernode's HTTP router still routes per-chain requests at `/<chainID>/`, but the per-chain handler passes through several states:

1. **VN stopping.** The handler is still registered but the inner op-node is tearing down its driver, P2P host, and event system. RPC methods return errors from the now-broken services.
2. **Container paused.** The chain container's restart loop is in its pause branch (`chain_container.go:315-325`, 1s sleeps). The previous incarnation's handler is still installed in the router; same error pattern.
3. **Fresh handler swapped in.** When `Resume` fires, the loop creates a brand-new `oprpc.Handler` and `setHandler`s it into the router (`chain_container.go:287-290`). For a brief window the handler exists but the new inner op-node hasn't yet called `registerAPIs`, so requests get JSON-RPC method-not-found responses.
4. **Inner op-node booted, APIs registered.** Steady state resumes.

The transition takes seconds: it's bounded by `vn.Stop`'s 30s timeout plus the rewind work plus the new VN's startup. We haven't measured the distribution precisely, but it's long enough for a poll-driven consumer running at second granularity to observe several failed polls in tests.

## Proposed change

Add per-chain readiness gating to the supernode's RPC router. The router already holds a `chainID → handler` map; extend it so each chain also has a "ready" state. When the chain container marks a chain not-ready (before stopping the VN), new requests for that chain block in the router rather than being immediately dispatched to a broken handler. When the chain container marks the chain ready again (after the new VN finishes booting), blocked requests proceed against the fresh handler.

Requests stay bounded by the caller's context deadline — if the gate stays open longer than the client's RPC timeout, the request fails with a connection-level error as usual. For comparison, op-conductor's default `ConductorRpcTimeout` is 5s; most rewinds should hopefully resolve inside that.

## Open design question: what defines "VN ready"?

The gate-close transition needs a signal from the chain container saying "the new VN has installed its RPC services and can serve real responses." Three options, in order of intrusiveness:

1. **Probe via the in-proc rollup client.** The chain container already wires up an in-process rollup client (`chain_container.go:294`). Spawn a short-lived goroutine after starting the new VN that polls a basic method (e.g., `SyncStatus`) until it succeeds, then close the gate. Pros: no op-node changes. Cons: indirect signal (probing rather than affirmation); a transient goroutine per restart.
2. **Callback from op-node's init path.** Plumb an `OnAPIRegistered` hook through `opnodecfg.Config` or `InitializationOverrides`. op-node calls it immediately after `registerAPIs` returns. Pros: deterministic and direct. Cons: small new op-node API surface.
3. **Event emitted by op-node on its existing event system.** The chain container subscribes. Most decoupled, most wiring for a single signal.

A reasonable starting point is option 1 (no op-node changes needed); upgrade to option 2 if probing proves flaky. Option 3 is more machinery than this signal warrants.

## Out of scope

- **Post-rewind staleness.** After the gate closes, `optimism_syncStatus` will truthfully return an `UnsafeL2.Time` far behind wall clock for a while. This issue is about RPC *availability*, not about masking stale-but-valid responses; consumers that care about lag/reorgs (op-conductor, dashboards) need their own tolerance for that.
- **Peer reconnection windows.** Once the gate closes, `opp2p_peerStats` will truthfully report low peer counts until peer discovery completes.

## Related

- #20006 — op-conductor reorg recovery deadlock (consumer-side symptom of the same root cause)

topPRs.title: feat(sdm): op-rbuilder + rollup-boost flashblocks support
topPRs.author: nonsense
topPRs.body:
Stacked on #21043.

Wires SDM PostExec through the flashblocks path:
- rollup-boost carries PostExec tx in flashblock frames
- op-rbuilder produces PostExec flashblock payloads + admin opt-in
- op-reth trait tightening to expose \`State<DB>\` to the builder

Brings the stack to functional parity with #20738.

topPRs.title: Add super permissioned dispute game support
topPRs.author: stevennevins
topPRs.body:
Adds the super permissioned dispute game implementation and wires game type 5 through contracts, deployment, proposer, dispute monitor, challenger, and migration validation paths.

The challenger now registers a dedicated super-permissioned actor that compares proposed super roots against supervisor/supernode data, challenges invalid games, and resolves valid games after the challenge window.

This also updates game argument encoding, deployment/manage flags, ABI/storage snapshots, and tests for the new simplified permissioned super-root flow.

Validated with `go test ./op-challenger/game/fault/contracts ./op-challenger/game/fault ./op-dispute-mon/mon/extract ./op-proposer/contracts ./op-chain-ops/interopgen ./op-deployer/pkg/deployer/manage`, `go test ./op-challenger/cmd ./op-challenger/config ./op-challenger/game/fault/contracts ./op-challenger/game/fault`, `forge test --match-contract SuperPermissionedDisputeGame --match-path 'test/dispute/SuperPermissionedDisputeGame.t.sol'`, and `DEV_FEATURE__OPTIMISM_PORTAL_INTEROP=true DEV_FEATURE__SUPER_ROOT_GAMES_MIGRATION=true forge test --match-contract 'OPContractsManagerV2_Migrate_Test|OPContractsManagerStandardValidator_Super|OPContractsManagerMigrationValidator'`.
